title: Microbial Biomarkers in Endometrial Cancer: Integrating Vaginal, Endometrial, and Gut Microbiota for Early Detection
content: Endometrial cancer (EC) is the most frequent type of gynecologic malignancy in the developedworld, and its prevalence keeps on increasing globally. Even though obesity, hormonal imbalance,and genetic susceptibility are known risk factors for the disease, new studies show that themicrobiome of humans could be responsible for disease pathogenesis and can provide usefulbiomarkers for the diagnosis. Sequencing technology allows identifying distinct changes in themicrobiome of the vagina, endometrium, and gut that correlate with EC. The changes typicallyinclude a reduction of beneficial Lactobacillus bacteria and an increase in the amount of anaerobicbacteria like Porphyromonas, Prevotella, Anaerococcus, Atopobium, Gardnerella, and Peptoniphilus. This review highlights current findings on EC-related alterations in the microbiomeand their possible mechanisms of action on cancer initiation by way of inflammation, immunesystem manipulation, impairment of the epithelial barrier, and estrogen metabolism. Additionally,the pros and cons of different methods of collecting samples, such as cervicovaginal swabs,endometrial tissue samples, uterine lavage, fecal material, and metabolomics, are outlined. Theissues facing the implementation of microbial biomarkers in clinical practice include a lack ofmicrobial biomass, contamination, heterogeneity of methods used, and limited external validation.Future work should be devoted to the standardisation of methodology, multi-centre studies ofvalidation, prospective cohort studies, and multi-omic analysis. In summary, microbial biomarkersare an exciting field that holds great promise for endometrial cancer.
